rv.q: Invictus mostly succeeds in creating a world where the very air feels thick with desire and regret, the two inextricably knotted together.
Nonetheless, the direction by Charles Askenaizer is uneven at times, and those performances don't always entirely connect with one another.
Watching her be ground down over the course of the play—she begins as an energetic naif and ends as just another emotionally scarred wretch—is utterly heartbreaking.
Director Charles Askenaizer transports us to the small Russian town filled with existential woe, philosophical debates on life and love, and bridges the centuries with this timeless classic.
For a smallish storefront theater like Invictus to do so well by a play as expansive and demanding as “Three Sisters” is no mean feat, and I wish the show a long and happy run.
It creates a space where naked, desperate emotions wash over the audience in waves.
It is a solid production that might be a little long for the average theater audience.

cn.t: Invictus Theatre's Chekhov adaptation earns mostly positive notices for strong performances and thoughtful staging, though uneven direction and a nearly three-hour runtime test patience. A worthy if imperfect take on a classic.
